%1$d file(s) in /system/etc/security/cacerts cannot be read by an ordinary app. Their permissions are not the ones the preinstalled roots have (0644, owned by root).

The certificates are still trusted - only this app cannot see them. That has a confusing consequence: an install skips the root because the file is unreadable, then the certificate installer refuses it because the root really is already trusted, so the run finishes having done nothing.

This is a fault of the device, not of a run. A root shell repairs it by giving those files the permissions of every other root:

chmod 644 /system/etc/security/cacerts/<name>
chown 0:0 /system/etc/security/cacerts/<name>

Installing into the SYSTEM store with root (2a) writes its own copies with those permissions.

Confirms the dialogs of the Android certificate installer while zhusheng installs certificates into the user store, and taps through the certificate list in the settings while it removes them again. Needs Android 4.1 or newer; on Android 4.0 the prompts have to be confirmed by hand. It only acts between the start and the end of such a run.
No accessibility settings found on this device.

zhusheng downloads the official root certificates published by the major TLS/SSL providers and installs them so that older Android devices (4.0 - 6.0) can again validate the certificates used by modern HTTPS websites.

Two install modes are available:

1) SYSTEM store (needs root): the certificates are copied into /system/etc/security/cacerts and are trusted by every app.

2) USER store (no root): each certificate is installed through the Android certificate installer. On Android versions below 7.0, certificates in the user store are trusted system-wide, so this also fixes HTTPS for all apps.

A reboot is recommended after installing into the SYSTEM store.
The app icon is fully human-made.

zhusheng was designed for Android 4.0 through 6.0, and this device runs a newer version.

Android 7.0 changed the way the system handles user-installed certificates: certificates placed in the user store are no longer trusted by apps that target Android 7.0 or newer. Installing into the USER store (2b) will therefore have no effect for most apps here.

Installing into the SYSTEM store (2a) may still work, but it needs root, and versions above 6.0 are beyond what zhusheng officially supports. Later releases changed the system certificate store further, so it may fail.
root (su) was not found. Use the USER store option instead, or grant root access.

Installed %1$d certificate(s) into /system/etc/security/cacerts. Reboot to apply.
System install did not report success.
What the marked lines above mean:
ZHUSHENG_COPIED — how many certificates were copied into the system store. Roots the store already held were left alone and are not counted.

ZHUSHENG_REMOVED — how many certificate files were deleted. In the system store these are the roots this app installed there; in the user store they are the files holding the certificates you selected. Roots that came with the device are never touched.
ZHUSHENG_DEDUPED — how many roots the system store held more than once. The extra copies were deleted and one copy of each was kept, so no certificate was lost.
ZHUSHENG_DONE — the script ran to the end. Without this line the script was interrupted.
system-installed.txt — the record of what this app installed was not found, so there was nothing it is allowed to remove.
could not write — the script could not be written into the cache directory of the app itself, so nothing was run at all.
command timed out — the root shell did not answer in time. Grant root access if a prompt is waiting and try again.
exec failed — the root shell could not be started at all. Check that su works on this device.
The script printed nothing at all. That is usually what a refused request for root looks like: nothing ran, so nothing was changed.

The certificates this app installed into /system/etc/security/cacerts will be deleted again. Roots that came with the device are left alone. A root the store holds more than once is reduced to a single copy as well. A reboot is recommended afterwards.
The certificates this app added to the user store will be deleted again. The user store has no API for removing a certificate, so this needs root.

Nothing to remove: none of the certificates that are loaded was found in that store.
Removing needs root. Without it, delete the certificate by hand under Settings > Security > Trusted credentials.

Without root a certificate in the user store can only be removed in the system settings:

1. Open Settings, then Security, then Trusted credentials - the button below takes you there.
2. Switch to the USER tab.
3. Tap the certificate you want to remove.
4. Confirm with OK or Remove.

The certificates this app installed are listed under the name of their CA, for example "ISRG Root X1". Wording and order differ a little between Android releases. A screen lock (PIN, pattern or password) may be asked for before a certificate can be removed.
No certificate list could be opened on this device. Open Settings > Security > Trusted credentials yourself.

The certificate list of the system settings will be opened and the auto-confirm service will remove the certificates that are loaded here from it, one row at a time.\n\nIt only taps rows whose name matches one of these certificates, and it stops as soon as this screen is in front again. You can take over by hand at any moment - the list stays where it is.
Removing %1$d certificate(s) through the settings screen…
Automatic removal stopped. Check the list if anything is left.
The user store has no API for removing a certificate, so what leaves it is decided by who does the deleting. Choose the way this device can take:
Delete the files with root (this device has none)

The files under /data/misc/user/0/cacerts-added (older releases: /data/misc/keychain/cacerts-added) are deleted directly. A file goes only when its content is one of the certificates loaded here. Needs root.
Remove by hand in the settings
The certificate list of the system settings is opened and you remove each certificate there: tap its row, press Remove, confirm. Nothing is deleted by the app, and this way needs no root.

That same list is opened, but the auto-confirm service taps the rows of these certificates and confirms what follows, so the run needs no attention. It has to be switched on in the system accessibility settings first, and it needs Android 4.1 or newer.
The certificates are installed through the Android certificate installer, which asks for confirmation. Choose how those prompts should go:
One prompt for the whole set
Every certificate is offered to the installer at once. Some Android 4.x builds read that and ignore it; the app then asks about one certificate after the other. You confirm the prompts yourself.
Each certificate gets its own dialog, and confirming one opens the next. Slower than the first option, but it behaves the same on every installer. You confirm the prompts yourself.
The auto-confirm service taps OK in every dialog, so the run needs no attention. It has to be switched on in the system accessibility settings first, and it needs Android 4.1 or newer.

zhusheng can answer the prompts of the certificate installer for you, but it may not switch on its own accessibility service - only you can do that, in the system accessibility settings.

While an install or a removal started by this app is going on, the service taps the OK button of the installer's dialogs and, during a removal, the rows of the certificate list in the settings. Outside such a run it does nothing at all, and it never touches a dialog another app opened.

The entry to switch on is called "%1$s".

Warning: the service works by tapping through screens quickly, and the display can flash repeatedly while a run is going on. If flashing lights are a problem for you (photosensitive epilepsy), use one of the ways that confirm by hand instead - neither of them needs a service.

The auto-confirm service is on. It answers the certificate installer\'s prompts and works the certificate list of the settings while this app removes certificates from the user store.\n\nSwitch it off in the system accessibility settings if you would rather confirm everything yourself.

Already trusted at the system level

Android keeps a certificate in one store only. These certificates are already in the SYSTEM store of this device, so the certificate installer reports success for them and adds nothing to the USER store:

%1$s

Nothing is broken and nothing was lost - they are trusted by every app already. To see them in the user store instead, remove them from the SYSTEM store first (3a) and install them again.
